report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Decisions About Expressing Subjective States Generalise Across Psychological Domains

text.text: People routinely make decisions about how to express their internal psychological states to the outside world.
These communication choices can systematically influence the meaning observers extract about the internal states of others.
In psychological science, this is frequently observed in the way people respond to self-report surveys.
Quantitative cognitive models of these communication choices, such as the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, translate continuous psychological states into Likert-type responses.
In doing so, the model can separate internal experiences (latent states) from preferences for (or against) certain response options in self-report scenarios.
A key assumption of the LASARS model is that response style reflects a stable individual characteristic that generalises across contexts.
The present study tested this assumption by examining whether response styles remain consistent across theoretically distinct psychological domains.
A sample of 145 adults completed four survey instruments assessing sensation seeking, thinking styles, dark personality traits, and perceived control.

We compared a model in which response style parameters were estimated separately for each instrument with a more parsimonious model in which response style was assumed to be identical across all instruments.
Response style parameters exhibited strong cross-instrument correlations, exceeding the magnitude of correlations observed among latent states.

Furthermore, constraining response style to be shared across instruments produced virtually identical predictions of observed scores and latent state estimates while reducing model complexity substantially.
These findings provide strong evidence that response style is a stable, domain-general characteristic.
They also support the conclusion that people use similar decision strategies to express their internal psychological states across the different constructs they may wish or be asked to communicate.
Survey responses are influenced not only by respondents' underlying latent statesfoot_0 , but also by the choices they make when communicating those states (Schwarz, 1999).

This finding is noteworthy because it suggests that the reliability and convergent validity commonly observed across psychological measures may reflect not only overlap in latent states, but also consistency in the ways individuals respond to rating scales.
However, whether response style remains stable across different psychological domains remains an open question.

This poses a more demanding test of the LASARS model, as the consistency observed within a single construct could alternatively reflect shared variance between latent states and response style, or construct-specific measurement artefacts.

text.text: Consequently, the extent to which response styles reflect domain-general individual differences, rather than context-dependent response tendencies, remains an important issue for establishing the validity and comparability of psychological measurement.

Furthermore, clarifying the range of contexts over which response style remains stable could inform the development of response style theory and provide clearer guidance regarding the analysis and interpretation of Likert-scale data.

In this paper, we investigate whether response style remains consistent across different psychological domains and, moreover, whether that consistency is sufficient to justify the assumption that individuals adopt the same response strategies across survey contexts.
We first demonstrate that response style is remarkably similar across a diverse range of instruments.
Guided by this finding, we then tested a more stringent psychological assumption: that people have the same response style across surveys.
We found that this more parsimonious approach neither diminishes the model's ability to accurately describe observed responses nor alters the substantive conclusions drawn from the data.
These findings provide support for the proposition that response style reflects a stable, domain-general characteristic of respondents.

text.text: The SD3 measures three aversive facets of personality -Machiavellianism, Narcissism and Psychopathy.

The original survey contains nine items for each of the three subscales, however, due to an administrative error, data from two machiavellianism and one psychopathy items could not be used in this analysis.

To facilitate direct comparison of response style across instruments, the response options for all measures were standardised to a common five-point Likert scale with the labels1 = Disagree,2 = Slightly Disagree,3 = Neutral,4 = Slightly Agree, and5 = Agree.
To test different assumptions about the consistency of response styles across different survey instruments, we tested two parameterisations of the model.
In the first, which we call the 'Separate' Model, we assume that people approach different surveys with different response strategies.

Under this specification, latent states were estimated for each construct measured across the four surveys, yielding a total of 10 latent state parameters (cf. rows in Table 1), while each of the four surveys was assigned its own set of three response style parameters (centre, odd, and directional responding), resulting in 12 response style parameters overall.

text.text: Thus, the Separate model comprised 22 person-level parameters in total.
In the second model, which we call the 'Shared' model, we assume that people adopt identical response strategies across all survey instruments.

Under this specification, the same 10 latent state parameters estimated by the Separate model were retained, but only a single set of three response style parameters was estimated and assumed to apply across all four survey instruments, resulting in a total of 13 parameters.
For both models, parameters were estimated using the Particle Metropolis within Gibbs (PMwG) sampling algorithm (Cooper et al., 2024; Gunawan et al., 2020).

text.text: Sampling consisted of 3,000 iterations of 50 particles for all three PMwG stages.
All analyses were conducted using samples from the final sampling stage only.
Standard multivariate normal priors with mean zero and an identity covariance matrix were specified for all person-level parameters.
The target particle acceptance rate was set to .95.
Reported correlations were derived from the estimated covariance matrix.

text.text: Contrasting the two LASARS models allowed us to directly test whether domain-specific response style parameters (measured by the Separate model) meaningfully improve model performance beyond a domain-general representation of response behaviour (measured by the Shared model).

To evaluate the extent to which response style parameters could be shared across instruments, we generated 100 posterior predictions for each participant from both the Separate and Shared models and averaged these across sampling iterations.
We then compared these predicted scores with the observed scale scores calculated with the conventional scoring method to test the respective models' abilities to reproduce observed responses.
We also ran preliminary checks to ensure that our changes to the survey response formats did not affect their normative interpretation.
To do this, we used what will henceforth be referred to as the 'conventional scoring method', whereby reverse-coded items are scored and responses are summed to create a scale score.
Although no widely accepted normative values exist for the REI, the observed scores fell within the range reported in previous research (McLaughlin et al., 2014).

Taken together, this result suggests that people's response strategies are remarkably similar across different survey instruments, even when the surveys measure relatively distinct psychological constructs.

Given the strong consistency of response style observed across psychological domains which are mainly distinct from one another, it may be reasonable to assume that individuals approach different survey instruments with the same underlying response preferences, at least when response formats are held constant.

To evaluate this possibility, we compared the Separate model with the Shared model, a more parsimonious variant of the LASARS framework in which response style parameters were constrained to be equal across all instruments.
This comparison allowed us to assess whether the additional complexity of estimating instrument-specific response style parameters yielded meaningful gains in predictive performance.

If the two models exhibit comparable predictive ability, the Shared model would be preferred on the grounds of parsimony, suggesting that a common response style process adequately characterises responding across instruments.

Given the substantial reduction in model complexity achieved by the Shared model (3 response style parameters instead of 12, for a total of 13 versus 22 person-level parameters), the absence of any meaningful loss in descriptive performance provides strong evidence that a common set of response style parameters can adequately characterise response behaviour across the set of survey instruments.
In many applications of survey research, the primary objective is to draw inferences about individuals' latent states.

Consequently, before concluding that the Shared model is appropriate, it is necessary to establish whether constraining response style parameters across instruments alters the substantive interpretation of these latent states.

text.text: These results indicate the simplifying assumption that people use the same response style across instruments has no meaningful impact on the discovery of individual differences in psychologically meaningful constructs.
In this paper, we examined whether decisions about communicating latent states are consistent across surveys measuring theoretically distinct psychological constructs.

We first demonstrated that, when response style parameters were estimated separately for each instrument, the resulting response style estimates were remarkably strongly correlated across tasks, despite the weak relationships observed between the latent states themselves.

We then evaluated the stronger assumption that individuals adopt the same response strategies across instruments by comparing a model with instrument-specific response style parameters to a more parsimonious model in which response style was shared across all measures.

Despite the substantial reduction in model complexity, there was virtually identical latent state identification between the Separate and Shared models, and the substantive conclusions drawn from the two were indistinguishable for all but one participant-latent state combination.

Taken together, these findings provide strong evidence that response style reflects a stable, domain-general tendency that can be modelled parsimoniously without compromising predictive performance or the interpretation of latent states.

These findings are consistent with a growing body of literature demonstrating that response styles exhibit substantial stability across both time (Weijters et al., 2010; Wetzel et al., 2016) and measurement contexts (Danner et al., 2015; Kieruj & Moors, 2013; Wetzel et al., 2013).

text.text: At first glance, these findings may appear to contrast with evidence from item-level modelling approaches (Ames, 2022; Bolt & Meng, 2025), which suggest that response behaviour can vary according to item and task characteristics.

text.text: However, the LASARS framework adopts a broader perspective, conceptualising response style as a three-dimensional signature of responding.

Although this signature may not be perfectly invariant across contexts, it appears sufficiently stable to be meaningfully characterised at the person level and to capture substantial variation in response tendencies across instruments.

Our results suggest that, although item and task characteristics may influence responding to some extent, these influences are generally insufficient to produce meaningful changes in the underlying response preferences that drive substantive conclusions about latent states, at least under the conditions tested here.
These findings have interesting theoretical implications for the study and understanding of response style.

Specifically, they suggest that response style is sufficiently consistent across distinct psychological domains to be treated as a common underlying tendency rather than a construct-specific artefact.

This result provides further support for the theoretical position that response style represents a meaningful source of individual differences (Grimmond, Brown, Gronau, & Hawkins, 2026a) and that the LASARS model's assumption of stability is appropriate, even in circumstances where the survey instruments measure largely theoretically distinct psychological constructs.

text.text: From this perspective, response style may capture information about enduring psychological dispositions in its own right, rather than simply reflecting measurement error or random response variability, as has been previously assumed (Baumgartner & Steenkamp, 2001).

text.text: Such an interpretation opens several interesting theoretical avenues for future research, including the possibility that response style is linked to broad personality characteristics, cognitive processing preferences, motivational factors, or habitual strategies for interacting with rating scales.

For example, Grimmond et al. (2025) found that extreme responders tended to be higher in all Big-Five personality traits (openness, extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness) except neuroticism, in which they were lower.

text.text: Understanding these relationships may ultimately provide insight not only into how people respond to surveys, but also into stable aspects of individual psychological functioning that are expressed through response behaviour.
These findings also have important practical implications for the measurement and analysis of Likert-scale data.

Our results suggest that, when response formats are equivalent, it is both theoretically and empirically justifiable to assume that individuals bring the same underlying response preferences to different survey instruments.
Broadly, the ability to estimate response style jointly across multiple instruments may help mitigate limitations associated with imperfect scale design.

For example, information about a respondent's response style obtained from a well-designed instrument, such as one with a balanced mixture of positively and negatively worded items, may assist in distinguishing response style from latent state variation in measures where aspects of response behaviour are more strongly confounded with construct measurement (e.g., directional responding; see Grimmond, Brown, Gronau, and Hawkins, 2026a).

This simplification also makes the model easier to apply in practice, as data from multiple instruments can be combined and analysed simultaneously within the lasars jamovi module (Grimmond, Hawkins, et al., 2026a) or R package (Grimmond, Hawkins, et al., 2026b).

Despite these implications, several limitations should be acknowledged.

Previous research has shown that characteristics of the survey instrument, such as the number of response categories, the labelling of response options, item wording, and overall scale structure, can all affect how respondents use rating scales (Kusmaryono et al., 2022; Leung, 2011).

text.text: Consequently, response style may reflect not only stable individual differences but also systematic features of the response format itself.
Because all instruments in the present study were administered using an identical response format, the current design cannot fully disentangle these sources of variation.

Although previous LASARS-based research suggests that response style remains largely consistent across tasks that differ in their response-option labels and category structures (Grimmond, Brown, Gronau, & Hawkins, 2026a), the extent to which this stability persists when both psychological domain and response format vary simultaneously remains uncertain.

text.text: Future research should, therefore, investigate the generalisability of response style across distinct constructs while systematically manipulating response formats.

Such work would provide a more stringent test of the domain-generality of response style and help identify the boundary conditions under which the assumption of response style stability remains appropriate.
It also remains unclear whether these findings generalise beyond the types of individual differences measures examined in the present study.

While the current results suggest that response style is highly stable across a range of psychological trait measures, other forms of self-report assessment may place different demands on respondents and, therefore, elicit different response behaviours.

For example, measures of preferences, confidence judgements, or attitudes may engage distinct cognitive processes, while surveys addressing sensitive topics may be more susceptible to socially desirable responding, impression management, or deliberate misreporting (Krumpal, 2013).

text.text: Such factors could weaken the consistency of response style observed across tasks and limit the generalisability of the present findings.

Future research should, therefore, investigate the stability of response style across a broader range of measurement contexts, including preferential judgements, confidence ratings, and attitudes towards socially sensitive issues, to better understand the conditions under which response style can be considered a domain-general individual characteristic.

In conclusion, the present findings provide strong evidence that response style is a stable and domain-general characteristic that extends across survey instruments assessing theoretically distinct psychological constructs.

When response style was estimated separately for each instrument, the resulting parameters exhibited remarkable consistency across tasks, despite the weak relationships observed between the latent states themselves.

Moreover, assuming a common response style across instruments produced virtually identical person-level latent state estimates and predictive performance while substantially reducing model complexity.

Together, these results support the central assumption of the LASARS framework that response style reflects an enduring aspect of how individuals interact with rating scales, rather than a task-specific source of measurement artefact.

More broadly, the findings suggest that response style should not be viewed solely as a nuisance variable to be controlled, but as a meaningful individual difference worthy of investigation in its own right.
We, therefore, encourage researchers to move beyond treating response style as a source of error and instead routinely measure, model, and report it alongside substantive psychological constructs.

Respondents are assumed to answer survey items by sampling from their latent state distribution and selecting the response option associated with the bin in which that sample falls.
Under this framework, survey responses are determined by two components: the location of the latent state distribution and the placement of the response thresholds.

The mean of the latent state distribution (µ) serves as a proxy for an individual's level on the underlying construct, with higher values corresponding to higher trait levels and a greater likelihood of selecting higher response options.
Response style is captured by the locations of the response thresholds, the placement of which is governed by three response style parameters, each representing a distinct aspect of responding.
Higher values of the centre preference parameter reflect greater overuse of middle response options.
The directional preference parameter captures asymmetry in responding, with higher values indicating a tendency towards selecting options on the right-hand side of the scale.

Finally, the odds preference parameter describes non-uniform use of response options, reflecting a general tendency to favour a combination of outer and middle options which, for a 5-point scale, corresponds with a preference for odd-numbered response options (i.e., 1, 3, and 5).
